summary: A fictional example. A shared grocery list for people who live together, which I designed with an AI agent: I set the direction and the cuts, the AI built and proposed options. It started as a meal planner and ended as the simplest list possible.

moments.title: A list, not a meal planner
moments.question: What problem does the app solve first?
moments.direction: I interviewed my flatmates: nobody plans meals, but everyone forgets what's missing at home.
moments.ai: Built a weekly meal planner with recipes that fed ingredients into a shopping list.
moments.decision: I cut recipes and planning and kept only the shared list. Planning can come later if anyone asks for it.
moments.why: The planner solved a problem my users didn't have. The list solves the one they have every week.
moments.quote: Nobody here plans meals. We just run out of things.

moments.title: Add items in one tap
moments.question: How much does it cost to add something to the list?
moments.direction: I timed myself adding five items: almost a minute, standing in front of the fridge.
moments.ai: Proposed a form with name, quantity, unit, category and store for every item.
moments.decision: I replaced the form with a single text field that understands "oat milk x2" and keeps recent items one tap away.
moments.why: If adding an item takes longer than remembering it, nobody adds it.
moments.quote: This should take two seconds, not a form.

moments.title: Who asked and who bought
moments.question: What do flatmates need to know about each item?
moments.direction: I noticed the real friction wasn't the list: it was not knowing who bought what, and who owed whom.
moments.ai: Showed a clean list where every item looked the same, with no owner.
moments.decision: I added a colored avatar for who asked for each item and a "bought by" mark when it's checked off.
moments.why: In a shared home, who bought it matters as much as what was bought.
moments.quote: The fights aren't about the milk, they're about who always buys it.

moments.title: A home, not a spreadsheet
moments.question: How should a shared-home app feel?
moments.direction: I gathered references from home and kitchen products and asked for something warm and calm, far from a productivity tool.
moments.ai: Proposed a high-contrast black and white theme with a dense layout.
moments.decision: I chose a warm paper tone with a deep green accent and more air between items.
moments.why: It's used at home, often in a hurry: it should feel like part of the kitchen, not like work.
moments.quote: It looks like a to-do app for work. This is our kitchen.

moments.title: One summary instead of every ping
moments.question: When should the app interrupt people?
moments.direction: Before sharing it with more homes, I tested it for a week with notifications on.
moments.ai: Sent a push notification every time anyone added or checked off an item.
moments.decision: I replaced them with a single daily summary at 6 pm, before people head home.
moments.why: An app that pings for every banana gets muted, and then the list stops working.
moments.quote: I got eleven notifications for one grocery run.
